Grandma, first question: where did you live when you were little?

In the imperfetto the stress falls on the vowel before V: par-LA-vo, leg-JE-vo, dor-MEE-vo.
With noi and voi the stress moves to "VA": par-la-VA-mo, par-la-VA-te. The other forms keep the stress on "LA".
With loro the stress goes back to "LA": par-LA-va-no, jo-CA-va-no (not par-la-VA-no!).
GE / GI = "je / jee", as in Romanian: je-LA-ti, jo-CA-vo. Not "ghe".
The imperfetto corresponds almost exactly to the Romanian imperfect (locuiam, mă jucam, era). You use it for:
La casa era piccola e fredda.
The house was small and cold.
Age, time, weather in the past
Avevo otto anni. Erano le tre. Pioveva.
I was eight. It was three o'clock. It was raining.
I was happy. I was afraid.
Good news for Romanians: where you'd say "locuiam, făceam, era" in Romanian, Italian almost always uses the imperfetto.
Take the infinitive without -re and add: -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano.
The imperfetto is the most regular tense in Italian. Even andare, venire, volere, potere are regular: andavo, venivo, volevo, potevo.
Fare, dire, bere use the old Latin stem (facere, dicere, bevere) — but the endings are the usual ones. Only "essere" is truly irregular.
4. C'era / c'erano and expressions of habit
"C'è / ci sono" becomes "c'era / c'erano" in the imperfetto:
There used to be a shop here.
Once upon a time there was a king…
ogni giorno / ogni domenica / ogni estate
da piccolo, da bambino, da giovane
when I was little, as a child, when I was young
"C'era una volta" is how all Italian fairy tales begin, like "Once upon a time".
5. Una volta e adesso: comparing past and present
To compare, put the imperfetto next to the present:
Children used to play in the street; now they play on their phones.
I used to live in Sibiu, now I live in Florence.
Don't confuse them: "Da piccolo andavo al mare" (a habit, many times) ≠ "L'anno scorso sono andato al mare" (once, finished). We'll work on the difference between the two tenses in the next chapter.

The children played in the street.

Did you drink milk in the evening?
My grandfather always said the same thing.

At the workshop's Christmas dinner, after his second glass of wine, Professor Bellini did something incredible: he talked about his childhood.
"I lived in San Frediano, a stone's throw from here. There were six of us in three rooms: my parents, my two sisters, my grandfather and me.
My father was a taxi driver and was always working, even on Sundays. My mother sewed dresses for the rich ladies of via Tornabuoni. We weren't rich, but we didn't lack anything.
My grandfather, on the other hand, was a restorer. He had a small workshop full of paintings, brushes and jars that stank. I adored him.
Every day after school I ran to him. He didn't talk much. He'd give me a tiny brush and say only: 'Look. And don't touch anything.'
So I spent hours watching. I watched him clean a face, find a colour lost under three hundred years of dirt. It seemed like magic to me.

On Sunday mornings, when my father was working, my grandfather took me to the Uffizi. Back then entry was free for children. We always stopped in front of the same Madonna by Filippo Lippi, and he would ask me: 'What do you see today?' Every Sunday I saw something new.

At school, on the other hand, I was a disaster. I was shy, I didn't talk to anyone and I drew in my exercise books during maths lessons. The teacher used to tell my mother: 'This boy lives on the moon.'
I didn't live on the moon. I lived in my grandfather's paintings.

When I was fifteen, my grandfather died. He left me his workshop and that tiny brush. I still use it today, for the hardest jobs. And every time I pick it up, I hear his voice: 'Look. And don't touch anything.'"
Nobody spoke for a long moment. Then Giulia raised her glass: "To the professor's grandfather!" And everyone, even Bellini, smiled.

"non ci mancava niente" = we didn't lack anything

Che lavoro faceva il nonno di Bellini?
